title: India Detects Omicron RF.5 Variant in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu as Officials Urge Calm
excerpt: Genome sequencing confirms the new COVID-19 sub-lineage in samples from Kadapa district, but health authorities say current evidence shows no increased severity over existing Omicron strains.
body:
• The Omicron RF.5 sub-lineage has been confirmed in four COVID-19 samples from Andhra Pradesh's Kadapa district after genome sequencing at the National Institute of Virology in Pune.
  • Tamil Nadu has also detected RF.5 in all sequenced COVID samples, while Andhra Pradesh has reported 16 cases and four deaths — all in patients with severe underlying conditions.
  • RF.5 evolved naturally from the JN.1 lineage through the LF.7 and PY.1.1.1 branches and is not a recombinant variant. The WHO is monitoring it under routine genomic surveillance.
  • Health officials at both the state and national level say there is no evidence RF.5 causes more severe illness than other circulating Omicron strains, and have asked the public not to panic.

India has identified the Omicron RF.5 sub-variant of SARS-CoV-2 in COVID-19 samples from at least two states, prompting a measured public health response that has emphasised vigilance over alarm. The detection was confirmed through genome sequencing at the National Institute of Virology (NIV) in Pune, with Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu both reporting the variant in recent weeks.

Andhra Pradesh Health Minister Y. Satya Kumar Yadav announced that four COVID-positive samples from Kadapa district had been sent to the NIV, and all four tested positive for RF.5. The state has reported 16 COVID-19 cases this month, including 12 detected by July 16, along with four deaths — each involving patients with severe pre-existing medical conditions.

What Is RF.5?

RF.5 is a sub-lineage of the Omicron variant that evolved naturally from the JN.1 variant through the LF.7 and PY.1.1.1 branches. Crucially, it is not a recombinant variant — meaning it did not arise from the merging of two different viral strains, a process that can sometimes produce more unpredictable mutations.

The World Health Organization is tracking RF.5 as part of its routine genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2. The variant has been identified in higher numbers in Singapore and several other Southeast Asian countries, but has not been flagged for elevated concern.

Dr. Vishnuvardhan, Andhra Pradesh's Director of Medical Education, said current scientific evidence provides no indication that RF.5 is more dangerous than other Omicron sub-lineages. Symptoms remain consistent with the broader Omicron family: sore throat, cough, fever, headache, nasal congestion, fatigue and body aches.

Tamil Nadu Confirms RF.5 in All Sequenced Samples

Tamil Nadu's health department separately confirmed that RF.5 was detected in all COVID-19 samples it sent for genome sequencing, reinforcing the sub-variant's presence across southern India. The state health department said there was no cause for panic but urged continued vigilance and basic precautionary measures.

At the national level, Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda stated that the variant was not of concern based on available evidence, while confirming that the government was monitoring the situation closely. The remarks came as India's overall COVID-19 caseload remains at sporadic levels — a far cry from the devastating waves of 2020-2021.

Immunity Wall Holds Firm

Experts point to India's layered immunity — built through vaccination campaigns, booster doses and natural infection from prior waves — as a key reason new sub-variants have not translated into surges of severe illness. According to the WHO's latest global risk assessments, currently circulating sub-lineages related to the JN.1 family have not demonstrated an inherent capacity for more aggressive pathology.

"COVID-19 cases in Andhra Pradesh are sporadic, and the government is fully prepared to handle the situation."

— Y. Satya Kumar Yadav, Andhra Pradesh Health Minister

What Diaspora Communities Should Know

For Indians abroad planning travel to India or with elderly relatives in affected states, the current risk level remains low. Health authorities have confirmed that dedicated wards in teaching hospitals are ready, testing kits are stocked, and surveillance systems are operational. The standard travel precautions — masking in crowded settings, hand hygiene and staying current on boosters — apply, but there is no official advisory against travel.

What's Next

State health departments in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu have strengthened district-level surveillance and reviewed emergency response plans. Hospitals have been instructed to maintain readiness with isolation facilities, testing capabilities and medical supplies. The NIV will continue sequencing positive samples to track any further evolution of RF.5 or the emergence of additional sub-lineages. For now, the message from Indian health officials remains consistent: stay alert, follow basic precautions, but do not panic.
